chess.lede:
<!--@chess.lede-->Check-Mate is a chess board that plays against you on its own. A sensor
                 grid reads where the pieces are, and a CoreXY gantry carries an electromagnet
                 under the board. The engine is H.G. Muller's micro-Max, which I adapted for the
                 board, and it runs on the Arduino itself with no computer connected.<!--/@-->
chess.sensors-intro:
Each square has a Hall effect sensor that detects the pieces. The Arduino reads
                 the sensors and moves the opposing pieces with the CoreXY gantry.
chess.access:
<!--@chess.access-->You can change the difficulty through search depth, so a beginner and a
                 stronger player both get a real game. When you pick up a piece, an LED matrix
                 under the board lights up its legal moves and the moves the engine rates best.
                 Every move is also announced out loud, so someone who can't easily read the
                 board across the table can still follow the game.<!--/@-->
chess.awards: Provincial finalist, Hydro-Québec Science Fair. OIQ (Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec) award for technical complexity, OCTAS Youth Innovation award, and a Université de Sherbrooke scholarship.
chess.revisions:
<!--@chess.revisions-->Over 18 months I prototyped three complete systems before the board
                 worked. The models below come straight from the CAD.<!--/@-->
chess.learned: What I had to work out The hardest part was system integration and fitting all the electronics in. It was the first time I'd worked under so many constraints at once. The motors, drivers and electromagnet all put electromagnetic interference on the sensor grid. Wiring, calibrating and reading 64 separate sensors took over 40 m of wire. I shielded every motor and sensor signal wire, and calibrated each sensor twice, once with no interference and once with magnets present. To fit everything, I mounted components on every surface, including under the hinged playing surface.
chess.movement:
<!--@chess.movement-->CoreXY is a compact but more complex way to get Cartesian movement,
                 and it's common in 3D printers. Both motors stay bolted to the frame, so none of
                 their weight moves. The downside is that neither motor drives X or Y on its own,
                 since every move combines the two. Drag the magnet, or drive one motor at a
                 time.<!--/@-->
chess.corexy-note:
<svg viewBox="0 0 26 14" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1 11 C 8 12, 16 8, 23 3 M23 3 L17 4 M23 3 L22 9"/></svg>
                driving one motor on its own moves the magnet diagonally
chess.sensing:
<!--@chess.sensing-->The Hall effect sensor under each square detects whether a piece is
                 there and also its polarity. Each sensor has three pins. Power and ground are on
                 shared rails, so only the signal leg is unique, and the 64 signals go through four
                 16-channel multiplexers before reaching the Arduino. Hover over a square to follow
                 its path.<!--/@-->
chess.mux-note:
<svg viewBox="0 0 26 14" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1 11 C 8 12, 16 8, 23 3 M23 3 L17 4 M23 3 L22 9"/></svg>
                the select lines are shared, so all four mux read the same channel at once
chess.engine: The chess part is a minimax engine by H.G. Muller that I modified for my board. I added difficulty through search depth, an LED grid for legal moves and an LED grid for best moves.
chess.engine-tree:
The engine searches a tree of possible future moves and picks the branch that
                 scores best for its side and worst for the opponent.
chess.heat-note:
Brighter squares are ones the search
                     looked at more often.
crc.lede:
<!--@crc.lede-->Over 8 months I developed John Abbott's robot for the Canadian
                 Robotics Competition. I built a swerve drivetrain and a dual claw that stacks and
                 moves game pieces and can move in all three axes independently of the drive
                 base.<!--/@-->
crc.swerve-what:
In a swerve drive, every wheel is powered and can also steer a full 360 degrees.
                 With the steering and drive of all four wheels synced, the robot can drive in any
                 direction without turning to face it.
crc.swap:
Each module is self-contained and held in by four bolts. With the
                 bolts out, the whole module drops out from below, and a new one goes in the same
                 way.
crc.claw:
The claw holds pieces without gripping them. Two arms on fixed pivots work
                 like chopsticks, one on each side, and each stays tangent to the game piece. So
                 swinging them pushes the piece side to side while it's held from both sides the
                 whole time. Stacked pieces score a multiplier, so placement has to be exact. This
                 motion adds some movement in the Y direction, which lines a piece up over the stack
                 while the base stays still. Drag the piece, or grab either arm.
crc.claw-note:
<svg viewBox="0 0 26 14" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M1 11 C 8 12, 16 8, 23 3 M23 3 L17 4 M23 3 L22 9"/></svg>
                  at either end of its travel, the near arm points straight down
rl.lede:
<!--@rl.lede-->This is the balance and driving controller for my wheel-leg biped. It's a
                 neural network I trained with reinforcement learning (PPO) in the MuJoCo
                 simulator. Training took about 25 million control steps, which works out to 69
                 hours of simulated driving.<!--/@-->
rl.demo:
<!--@rl.demo-->The player below replays the trained policy in simulation. The network
                 next to it is the actual trained network. Its 22,406 weights run in your browser
                 on the same sensor readings the simulated robot got, so the neurons that light up
                 are the ones producing each motor command. The clips marked Demo mode use a second
                 policy trained with the hardware limits removed, which I describe at the end of
                 this section.<!--/@-->
rl.network:
<!--@rl.network-->Every 10 ms the network takes 39 values and returns 6. It has no
                 memory between steps and no physics model. It's two hidden layers of 128 neurons
                 with tanh activations, and it maps the current state straight to motor
                 commands.<!--/@-->
rl.hips-note:
The hips are position controlled. A PD loop at 1 kHz turns each
                     target into a torque, through a 12:1 3D-printed planetary gearbox. The wheels
                     are commanded in torque directly. The wheels do the balancing, and the legs set
                     the ride height and take up uneven ground.
rl.norm:
<!--@rl.norm-->The inputs are normalized with statistics collected during training, and
                 the network only works with those exact statistics. If the weights get exported
                 without them, the export still passes its own check but the robot behaves
                 wrongly. That happened once, so the export script now won't run without the
                 matching statistics file.<!--/@-->
rl.export:
<!--@rl.export-->The weights also export to a C header for the microcontroller. I checked
                 the C forward pass against the Python network, and the outputs match to within
                 4×10<sup>−7</sup>.<!--/@-->
rl.ppo:
<!--@rl.ppo-->PPO trains the network from experience. Six copies of the simulator
                 run in parallel with the policy driving each one, and every control step gets a
                 reward score. After each batch, the network is updated toward the actions that
                 scored better than expected. PPO limits how much a single update can change the
                 policy, which keeps training stable.<!--/@-->
rl.curriculum:
<!--@rl.curriculum-->Training uses a curriculum. It starts on flat ground with an ideal
                 robot that's mostly asked to stand still. Over the first 40% of training, the
                 terrain gets rougher, the pushes get harder, and the robot's physical parameters
                 are randomized over wider ranges.<!--/@-->
rl.learned: What I had to work out Partway through one run, episode length dropped from 1860 to 1160 steps. It looked like the normal dip when the curriculum gets harder, but it was a bug. The crouch command limit had been calculated from nominal motor values, and once the randomization widened, 92.5% of the simulated robots physically couldn't hold the commanded pose. I only found it by checking why episodes ended, not just how long they lasted. A second bug computed the velocity reward in the world frame instead of the robot's frame, so it measured the wrong axis whenever the robot turned. Forward speed tracking was stuck at 52% of the command until I fixed it.
rl.sim2real:
<!--@rl.sim2real-->A policy trained on one perfect simulated robot won't work on the real
                 one, so I made the simulation harder than reality on purpose. The motor model
                 uses the measured electrical constants, with a back-EMF torque limit and a
                 1 A current limit, and the windings heat up with use. Each episode also uses a
                 different randomized robot.<!--/@-->
rl.status: Current status The controller isn't finished yet. Under nominal conditions it balances, drives, turns in place and recovers from pushes. Turn rate tracks within a few percent, but forward speed only reaches about two thirds of a fast command, which you can see on the speed gauge in the player. It doesn't follow ride height commands yet. With full randomization it still fails about half of its 20 second episodes, and it can't reliably drive off an 18 mm step. Next I'm doing more validation in simulation, then testing on the real robot.
rl.demo-lede:
<!--@rl.demo-lede-->The policy above is limited by what my hardware can do. For this
                 version I kept training the same policy in a simulation with the physical limits
                 removed, to see how far the method could go when motor power wasn't the
                 constraint. These are the Demo mode clips in the player. It's only a simulation
                 result and won't be used on the real robot.<!--/@-->
rl.demo-result:
<!--@rl.demo-result-->I trained it for another 8 million steps, which took 3.5 hours. It
                 turns at 5.8 rad/s when asked for 6.0, stays up after 1 m/s pushes, and drives
                 over 24 mm steps. The hardware-limited policy fell on 18 mm steps in all
                 8 test runs. Episode survival went from about 50% to 81%.<!--/@-->
rl.demo-limits: What didn't improve Forward speed still undershoots, reaching 1.24 m/s when asked for 1.8, and it still doesn't follow ride height commands. The hardware-limited policy has both of these problems too, so they aren't caused by a lack of torque. A push that lands while it's driving and turning at the same time still knocks it over in five of six runs.
